newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds recoup some losses, eyes on U.S.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds recoup some losses, eyes on U.S.

text.p: Irish bonds recouped some of their earlier losses in the 10-year area in thin late trade on Wednesday as U.S. Treasuries edged mildly higher but further losses are seen along the curve in Ireland, dealers said.
Treasuries edged higher after U.S. December durable goods order fell 1.7 percent, versus forecasts for a 1.2 percent rise and a revised 1.7 percent fall in November.
The long bond was up 2/32 to yield 6.92 percent by 1535 GMT from 6.96 earlier, dealers said.
"We had fairly good numbers from the States earlier but the reaction was poor enough really. I am of the belief that we will see the Fed raise interest rates next week," one dealer said.
"My own belief is that we will see markets drift lower along the curve," he added.
By 1610 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 23 pence from Tuesday's close at 102.50 to yield 5.87 percent.
The key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was down 20 pence from the previous close at 109.35 to yield 6.53 percent, having been at 109.28 at 1030 GMT on Wednesday.
Dealers said Irish bonds were trading at 140 basis points over German bunds in the five-year area and 85 basis points over bunds in the 10-year area.
"We seem to be near the top end of our range again. We have been trading between 82 and 95 basis points over bunds in the 10-year area over the last couple of months," one dealer said.

News that Ireland's largest trade union, SIPTU, had voted on Wednesday to accept the latest wage agreement between employers, government and unions, a cornerstone of Ireland's economic success in recent years, had little impact on the market, dealers said.

"The news brought relief more than anything else," the dealer said. "But the U.S. is dominating what is happening in international markets. With rate rises likely in the U.S. and the UK and the dollar on the slide, it is looking bad for peripheral markets like Ireland," the dealer added.

The release of U.S. Q4 GDP data on Friday, with forecasts for a 3.9 percent rise compared to 2.1 percent, was of most immediate concern to the market while next week is likely to be dominated by the meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
